content: The studies described involve various methodologies and participant groups to investigate the effects of breastfeeding duration and other factors on health outcomes. Below is a professional summary of the key details: 1. Vehapoglu 2017: This cross-sectional study recruited 5,000 Turkish children aged 2–14 years from outpatient clinics in Istanbul between June 2012 and July 2014. The sample was ethnically and socioeconomically homogenous. Children with cardiovascular or endocrine diseases, preterm births, low birth weight, or congenital conditions were excluded. Breastfeeding practices were assessed, including duration and the introduction of formula or solid foods. Outcomes included BMI categories (underweight, normal weight, overweight, and obese). 2. Villamor 2000: Conducted in Tanzania, this cross-sectional study analyzed 161 children aged 6–60 months admitted with pneumonia. Data on anemia, hemoglobin levels, socioeconomic status, malaria, HIV, breastfeeding, and nutritional status were collected. Children were followed for at least one year post-discharge to assess survival, health, and growth. 3. Villegas 2008: A prospective cohort study in Shanghai examined women aged 40–70 years. Data on breastfeeding duration and reproductive history were collected through interviews. Breastfeeding duration was categorized, and its relationship with health outcomes was analyzed. 4. von Kries 1999: This cross-sectional study in Bavaria, Germany, evaluated 134,577 children during mandatory health examinations before school entry. Parents of 13,345 children completed questionnaires on atopic disease risk factors. BMI percentiles were used to define overweight and obesity. 5. Walby 2016: A retrospective cohort study in Sweden analyzed infants born between 2002 and 2007. Data on breastfeeding status at various ages were collected. Children with missing growth or breastfeeding data were excluded. 6. Wiklund 2012a: Part of the Calex family study in Finland, this retrospective cohort study included mothers with pre-pregnancy anthropometric data. Breastfeeding duration was categorized into quartiles, representing cumulative lactation experience. 7. Wong 2017: This cross-sectional study in Toronto, Canada, included healthy urban children aged 1–6 years attending routine healthcare visits. Breastfeeding duration was modeled as both a continuous and categorical variable. 8. Wong 2018: Another cross-sectional study in Toronto focused on healthy children aged 3–6 years. Breastfeeding duration was categorized, and its effects on cardiometabolic risk were assessed. 9. Yang 2017: This cross-sectional study in China involved 512,891 participants aged 30–79 years. Data on breastfeeding duration and reproductive history were collected. Outcomes included BMI, fat percentage, and waist circumference. 10. Yeo 2016: Based on the Korea National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, this study excluded individuals with chronic diseases or recent pregnancies. Breastfeeding duration per child was calculated, and its relationship with bone mineral density was analyzed. 11. Zhang 2015: This cross-sectional study in Beijing included parous women aged 40–81 years. Breastfeeding duration was categorized, and its association with hypertension and diabetes was examined. 12. Zhu 2020: A prospective cohort study followed 745 adolescents aged 10–12 years who were part of a birth cohort. Detailed breastfeeding data were collected during infancy. Cognitive development outcomes, including verbal comprehension, perceptual reasoning, working memory, processing speed, and full-scale IQ, were assessed. Excluded Studies: Several studies were excluded due to not focusing on continued breastfeeding or its duration. Reasons included analyzing exclusive breastfeeding, case-control designs, or using breastfeeding duration as a continuous variable without specific categorization. This detailed overview highlights the diverse methodologies and populations studied to explore the impact of breastfeeding and other factors on health outcomes.
